   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: Ken Stearn, FIFE

Dear Brian,

Many thanks for your reply,
printed in OUTLET Issue no. 54,
to my question on downloading
fonts to a 24-pin printer.
Unfortunately, I am still unable
to get the printout I require. I
used your program but just got
normal printing. The fonts I
have are the ones that came with
OUTWRITE and I tried them as 8
and 16 bit to no avail.

I am much clearer about the
whole business now but I wonder
if you could explain the
difference between 8 and 16-bit
fonts?

I tried a Font designer in
ENCELADUS Issue No. 5 and was
successful in printing a
downloaded font from within the
program but the font was stored
as a $ array. What is the
difference between this and a
font stored as code?

       Yours sincerely,

          Ken Stearn

Brian Cavers to Ken Stearn

The OUTWRITE character sets are
for use on-screen in OUTWRITE
itself and are nothing to do
with printing. Most people have
their own personal taste in text
style, some like a square,blocky
character, some like a thick,
rounded one while others like a
thin, spindly text.

The difference between the 8-bit
and 16-bit characters as used in
OUTWRITE are as follows...

An 8-bit set stores the design
of each letter on an 8 by 8 dot
matrix. For example, the letter
"A" might be stored as shown at
the top of the next page...

........                00000000
.oooooo.                01111110
.oo..oo.                01100110
.oo..oo.      or, in    01100110
.oooooo.      binary =  01111110
.oo..oo.                01100110
.oo..oo.                01100110
........                00000000


In Mode 1, the SAM would display
such a character on screen as
tiny, almost invisible, dots and
each dot or space would be repr-
esented by one bit.

Eight bits are stored in one
byte in each memory address and
each byte would appear on screen
as a row of eight horizontal
dots (or spaces),e.g., 01100110.

In Mode 3,each dot on the screen
is represented by TWO bits as it
has to include colour data so
TWO bytes are needed to store
each horizontal slice of eight
dots which make up the character
design. In BASIC, the standard
SAM character set is 8-bit and
so the routine that PRINTs the
characters on the screen has to
make adjustments for each dot
and this slows the routine down.
In OUTWRITE,the character design
is already changed into a form
that can be directly used and so
you will find OUTWRITE prints up
a screen of text faster than SAM
BASIC.The trade-off is more mem-
ory is used. A 16-bit equivalent
of 01100110 is 00111100 00111100
(if INK 3 on PAPER 0).
                         - Brian

From: Stuart Burton, POOLE

I was most interested in your
reply to Reg Jeffs in last
month's OUTLET. I too have
puzzled as to how to print
UDG's. My joy at being able to
print them is, however, tempered
by the problem of getting them
printed where you want them.

The PRINT AT and TAB commands do
not seem to work for UDG's and
also the NLQ for my CITIZEN
120D+ doesn't double-print the
UDG's.

Incidentally,the REVERSE LISTING
BUG has never happened to my
programs since incorporating
MASTERBASIC and MASTERDOS.

I believe Andy Wright has inc-
luded the "cure".Another reason
for buying these excellent
programs.

        Yours sincerely,

         Stuart Burton

Brian Cavers to Stuart Burton

LPRINT AT and TAB only work in
"expanded" ("text") mode - that
is, after using OPEN #3;"T".They
do not work after using OPEN #3;
"B" which you use to send binary
control codes. So, to use them
with high-res graphics you need
to first send the TAB using "T"
then the graphics with "B",e.g.:

10 CLOSE #3
20 OPEN #3;"T"
30 LPRINT TAB 50;
40 CLOSE #3
50 OPEN #3;"B"
60 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"K";CHR$ 8;
   CHR$ 0;
70 FOR N=UDG"A" TO UDG"A"+7:
   LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N;: NEXT N

NLQ on printers relates only to
the printer's own, built-in,text
characters. When you send high-
res graphic data you are taking
over control of your printer and
you, yourself need to send codes
and data for higher resolution.


If you look in your printer man-
ual you will see their are four
different resolutions(densities)
for high-res graphics: "K"(which
we used in our previous example)
"L", "Y" and "Z". The highest is
"Z" which gives quadruple densi-
ty but you must also then send
each piece of UDG data FOUR
TIMES after sending the "Z" code
as in the example on the next
page...

10 CLOSE #3: OPEN #3;"B"

20 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Z"; CHR$ 32;
   CHR$ 0;:REM send 32 pieces of
               data instead of 8

30 FOR N=UDG"A" TO UDG"A"+7

40 FOR M=1 TO 4:REM send 4 times

50 LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N;

60 NEXT M

70 NEXT N


(Anyone who didn't see last
month should note that the UDG
is rotated and mirrored compared
to how it will show on-screen.)

If anyone wants to print eight
or more UDGs together then you
might not know how to calculate
the two values at line 20 that
state how much high-res data is
about to be sent to the printer.
An easy way to calculate is,eg.,
for 12 UDGs...

10 RANDOMIZE 32*12:REM (12 UDGS)
20 LET LO=PEEK 23670
30 LET HI=PEEK 23671

         and then use...

50 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Z";CHR$ LO;
   CHR$ HI

For less than 8 UDGS you can use
32 times the number of UDGS for
the first CHR$ and 0 for the
last.

It's also worth stating here
that although most printer man-
uals show the value for CHR$ in
brackets, e.g., CHR$ (27), both
SAM and Spectrum BASIC are more
advanced than many BASICs in
this respect and you do not need
the brackets UNLESS it is a
calculated value, for example:
CHR$ (X*3+2).

Thanks for the tip about the
reverse listing bug. I am start-
ing to use MASTERBASIC more now
so your advice may push me more
in that direction. I've also
heard that MASTERBASIC cures the
infamous paging bug so long as
the program has NEVER been edit-
ed in SAM BASIC (ever!).
                          Brian

From: Tim Hards, BURY ST EDMUNDS

Dear Ron and Brian,

Now I have my computer, I will
be able to start experimenting
with PRODOS, especially with the
various computer languages that
can be used with it. From what I
have used so far it seems pretty
good. Do you or any of your
readers know how to transfer
files from a PRODOS disk to a
SAMDOS one?

On my SEIKOSHA SK-92 printer, if
I hold ON-LINE down when
switching on it does a little
printout giving the current
dip-switch settings. This is not
mentioned in the manual.

Of more interest is the fact
that to highlight the settings
it uses outlined characters
which is also not mentioned in
the manual. Now I'm wondering if
I can print outlined text. Do
you know what the printer code
is for this is on printers that
have that function?

I recently bought a MITSUBISHI
CT-1535 TX television with SCART
input. When I connected it the
computer screen was rolling. I
remembered reading about SCART
televisions in previous OUTLETs,
so set about going through all
of the letters looking for info.
I found a couple of letters
saying to replacing the resistor
in the SCART lead (monitor end)
with a BA157 diode.

So I did and now I have a wond-
erful, clear image (and better
sound). Thank you.

A suggestion I have is to add an
index to the end of OUTLETTERS
of all the topics covered in the
letters. This would have been
really handy when searching for
the SCART info.

In the latest Issue of OUTLET,
someone mentioned about convert-
ing TIFF picture files ffom PCs.
Coincidently, the day before I
had managed to crudely convert a
TIFF file. I saved a scanned
image from a school nimbus to a
blank disk so that it was stored
near the beginning (I do not
know how PC directories are
structured).

Through examination, it seems
there are two pixels per byte,
the same as for the Coupe. Of
course, the width and height are
different. They may even vary
from picture to picture, so
information is probably held
just before or just after the
graphics part, along with the
palettee info. I will examine
the data more closely later, and
if I discover how all the
information is stored, I will
get back to you.

             Yours,

           Tim Hards

From Brian Gaff to Tim Hards

It should not be too hard to
construct a Pro-Dos-to-Samdos
converter as you could use READ
AT and WRITE AT. I cannot go
into great detail here about the
Pro-Dos format, but this may
help you a bit.

The disc has 9 sectors per track
and there are 256 directory
spaces.Each one holds the track/
sector for up to 16K of the file
- in other words, a file of 17K
would need 2 directory entries.
The bytes 16 to 31 are called
the extents and hold the block
numbers used by the file. This
is in the Pro-Dos manual in more
detail.Remember the format has
alternating sides though!

As an aside, anyone who has
Pro-Dos that signs on with V1.7,
should contact me by phone, as
an upgrade is available.
(081 397 0763 after 7pm)

Outline printing is defined in
last month's Drivechat as being
ESC q. Note the lower case. The
features you mention are also
found on a CBM printer I saw
recently. It's a much more
civilized way of doing things!

Ah, the dreaded SCART. I must be
lucky, as my Fidelity works
perfectly with the SAM. Have you
tried removing the aerial from
the TV? If this does not work,
then I think you should try to
talk to Adrian Parker at SAMCO.
He says that some SCARTs need

linked pins at the SAM end - the
problem is that what you link
depends on what the EXACT
symptoms are... So much for
standardization. Be careful
though, as random experiments
could cause damage.
                           B.G.

subjects which I may publish as
it develops. I would dearly love
a complete index but cannot get
round to it no matter what!
Sorry!
                            B.C.

From.Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

Dear All,

Just after I posted the disc
with a letter that in part had
some notes relating to OMNICALC
2 I found some further info that
relates to a comment on the
program by Dr Gerard Behr. I
have found the program can be
used on SAM under the "SPECLONE"
emulator from Steve's Software.

This program   is one that needs
your own 48K Spectrum ROM.

Load the emulator select RESET
SPECTRUM (RAND 0) then load the
programme from tape in the
normal Spectrum way.

When LOADed press the "snap" or
"break" button on back of SAM to
return you to emulator menu.
(dont press reset in error!).
You can now "save Spectrum
memory" to disc.

To return to program select
"return to Spectrum" and enter
GOTO 1 to restart the program.
Do not use RUN and do not be
confused that the program screen
is present.

The program will now SAVE and
LOAD data to tape only from
within the program as there is
not any MD for the program to
recognise these functions.
However,it seems to print out ok
via SAM printer from the "P"
option.

I have tried the Disciple
version of the program but again
only tape seems to be useable as
there is no Disciple ( or +D )
ROM or DOS for the program to
call upon in SAM.

I am fairly certain both MD and
+D drive functions must be via
HOOK / COMMAND codes direct to
the apropiate ROM / DOS which is
obviously why they do not work.
I do not go in for Spectrum
emulators seriously so have no
idea if there is one that will
recognise +D disc command
functions in Spectrum mode.
It seems that the program can be
exited at any time with the
"break" button and the memory
dumped to disc which is the
equivilent of +D "snap".

Also the "snap" can be reLOADed
into the emulator but must be
restarted by GOTO 1 (not RUN).
I should warn it does seem a bit
too easy to crash the system but
I was not using the program
seriously so that could have
simply been my doing.


SPECLONE is available on DISC
ref SC_PD1 for `1.50
from: Steve's Software, 7 Narrow
Close, HISTON, CAMBRIDGE CB4 4XX

SAM NETWORK:
I presume you have found the
following:

V3 ROM  Unbooted SAM.
DEVICE N (or n1, n2 etc)

SAVE "xx" Now exits via network
socket.

I presume LOAD "" looks for
Programme via network.

All normal SAVEs and LOADs seem
to be via Network.

BOOT DOS v2. Network no longer
seems to work!!!

BOOT MASTERDOS. Network works as
for unbooted SAM.

Plus SAVE "N:xx" also works. I
presume all rest of normal SAVE
and LOAD also  work in this
form.

But SAVE "N1:xx" still tries to
use disc. (or N2, N3  etc)

Disciple data speed is some 2 -
3 times faster than SAMs on
networks.

None of Disciples network func-
tions seem to work with SAM.

Both are at TTL levels but won't
seem to talk to each other.

Extracted from TEC Manual:

1) Used by print a number
routine.
SYS VARS - 5BB5k - holds
destination net station no.

(not found anything to say how
to set a SAM station no. unless
it uses a variable normally
used with disc).

2) "BASIC INTERPRETER uses
common header format for 'T'
(Tape) 'D' (Disc) or 'N' (Net)".

Only having one SAM does
restrict typing to try out
Network.

         All the best,

            Malcolm

P.S.

Both Network sockets seem to be
in parallel as data exits via
both  at the same time.(I don't
know why 2 pins are shown linked
on one end and not other. Data
comes out of 1 and 7. - unless
the  other two are 'data in?')

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Perry

Ah great! Now you've said the
magic word "DEVICE" it all makes
sense. I should have thought of
that myself. The SAM User Guide
index does not include page 140
under "network". On this page it
clearly shows how to set the
Station number with e.g....
DEVICE N5 for Network Station 5

Page 153 says up to 16 SAMs can
be linked and Channel 0 is the
main broadcast station. This is
set up with DEVICE N0 but I
guess that DEVICE N will default
to that. Good - now we have the
complete picture. I wish I had
a cable and two SAMs in the same
room to try it!
                        - Brian

           Brian Gaff
          B.G. SERVICES
         64 Roebuck Road
           Chessington
         Surrey, KT9 1JX

       (Tel: 081 397 0763)

Hi Brian,

         I thought a little
update on Pro-Dos might be of
interest, so here we go.

Bugs...

Is there any program that is
free from these?

Anyway, so far we have been
fairly lucky, and only two have
shown up.

1) Anyone with V1.7 could have
trouble with lost characters on
printing if the printer buffer
overflows. This has been cured
in V1.8.

2) Both V1.7 and V1.8 have a
minor bug in the error routine.
The effect only shows itself if
a running program tries to write
to a file that has had the
PROTECT attribute set. The
effect is an INTERNAL ERROR
report, and an exit from the
program back to Pro-Dos. No real
harm occurs, and the fix is to
UPROTECT the file.

V1.9 will cure this by giving an
error FILE IS READ ONLY, and
then continuing with the
program.

UPDATES and PD

The PD sampler is now at V2.1
which includes a runable
tutorial aimed at explaining the
operations of some programs to
those not familiar with CP/M.
The DOCment file for ZDE is now
included, as is an UNDELETE
program.

FDOS PD now has 6 PD discs
available at `2  and 1 at `1.
Contact FDOS for full details.

STRANGE HAPPENINGS.

A couple of reports have reached
my ears that all 1Mb RAM packs
are not created equal! If you
have one of these add-ons, and

you think ProDos is misbehaving,
switch off and try it without
the 1Mb unit. There is nothing
wrong with Pro-Dos, as most 1Mb
users get on OK. My guess is
that a fault exists on some
packs that allows it to be
switched in when it should not
be. Hopefully, the two I have
heard of are just isolated
cases.

If anyone trashes their BOOT
disc or requires the latest
version, please ring me and I
wull provide you with an address
to send it to.

                     Brian Gaff.

From: A. de B. Adam, WOKING

Thank you for continuing with
"OUTLET". Please can you help me
to get more satisfaction from
your programs in the following
ways.

Can you let me know how to ex-
tract the individual programs so
I can file them under particular
headings for quicker extraction
and use. I have a +D Interface
and drive from Datel but do not
know how to use it properly.
With your permission, can you
please allow me to extract pro-
grams on fractals and introduce
colour and variations to them
and explain to me how to extract
them?
                       -Arthur

Brian Cavers to Arthur de B Adam

Yes, press BREAK (ESC on the SAM
Coupe) and enter BASIC (select
128K or +3 BASIC if a 128K
machine). To re-save the program
put a disc in the drive or start
the tape and enter...

 RUN 9972   (+3)

 RUN 9982   (+D,M/Drive,Opus)

 RUN 9983   (tape)

 RS         (SAM Coupe)

Occasionally some programs are
invisible or garbled when listed
in 128K so don't LOAD them but
merge them with MERGE..."name"

When reloading, if the message,
"file not found" appears (or if
a tape version is waiting to
load another file) then press
BREAK (ESC on SAM) and note down
the line number shown at the
bottom of the screen. e.g., 9010
in this example...

   L BREAK into program 9010:1


Enter LIST 9010 to see what file
needs to be copied. Use the COPY
command on +3 and SAM or SAVE TO
on +D and Disciple(see manuals).
These may also be used with the
main BASIC program if preferred.
If anyone needs any help with a
particular program,please write
to me.

Yes, you can certainly extract
programs on fractals or any
others you like. Feel free to
BREAK into OUTLET programs and
modify them as much as you like
for your own use. Remember, you
must not give away or sell any
OUTLET programs unless they are
marked "FREEWARE" or public
domain but you can extract them,
alter them, adjust them and re-
save them for your own use.

Some programs are machine code
and cannot be modified or listed
by beginners. Experience is
needed to modify even BASIC and
if you don't even know how to
BREAK into and extract programs
then you may not be able to
rewrite them to any great extent
-but experiment and learn!-Brian

From: J. Hunter, "Westward Ho"
   Church Close, Ogmore-by-Sea
     Mid Glamorgan CF32 0PW

Dear Brian,

Thank  you  for  publishing  my
effort about EASTER SUNDAY in
OUTLET Issue No. 55. I have now
tidied up the program. You are
quite right in pointing out
about typing in the program [as
a listing in the letter]  as I
managed to get an error in LINE
950 in which I typed:
LET C=Z-(100+B)
This should have read:
LET C=Z-(100*B)
i.e. the plus sign should have
been a multiply sign (poor use
of the SHIFT key!!!).

In the EASTER SUN program I have
made liberal use of REM state-
ments which try to explain the
mathematics used to arrive at
the end result.

All this arose from an article
in a publication called "PUZZLES
AND PARADOXES" which I came
across many years ago. The
computations therein were of an
arithmetic nature which I have
translated to computer language.
I wouldn't know, therefore, if
it is copyright and consequently
proper or not to make use of
that article as I have done.

WHITAKER'S  ALMANACK  1984
EDITION  contains  a table of
EASTER SUNDAY dates from the
year 1500 onwards.

Therefore, it would be possible
to test results of any computer
program aspiring to cover pre-
1753 dates. I have these dates
on an OUTWRITE File if needed.

The program itself is a bit
basic (no pun intended!) but I
am no expert programmer and the
program itself does work.

Many thanks again for a tip-top
magazine and customer service.

            J. Hunter

P.S.  Can  you tell me what to
POKE to my printer (Brother
1109) to  force  it to give, say
50 or 60 characters per line of
text, with, say, a left hand
margin of 5 spaces?

Brian Cavers to J. Hunter

Thanks, John. I have put your
"EASTER SUN" in ADD-ENDERS this
month with a program from E.A.
Hughes called "EASTER" which you
might like to compare.

Use the following to print 50
characters a line with a left
margin of 5 spaces...

10 CLOSE #3   :REM avoids errors
20 OPEN #3;"B":REM send codes
30 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"l";CHR$ 5;:
   REM left margin of 5. "l" is
   lower case L (=Left!)
50 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Q";CHR$ 55;
   : REM right margin = 55
60 CLOSE #3:OPEN #3;"P":REM text
60 POKE SVAR 14,255: REM disable
   line length system variable


That final POKE is not strictly
necessary in that example but if
you ever try to print more than
80 characters on a line,say with
condensed text then that sysvar
may override your setting and
start a new line after 80 char-
acters so I generally disable it
as a habit. An alternative is to
use that sysvar itself...
         POKE SVAR 14,50
  ...instead of the right margin
setting. This gives a specific
line length of 50. However, I
think the sysvar itself is an
uneccessary nuisance - it's just
one more thing to think about
and the normal printer margin
codes work perfectly well and
are standard software on any
computer.
                        - Brian

From: E.A. Hughes, HEREFORDSHIRE

Dear Brian and Ron,

The letter from John Hunter in
Outletters, Issue No 55 has
prompted me to write this, my
first letter to you.

Some 8 or 9 years ago when I
bought my first SPECTRUM I prod-
uced my first Calendar program
of which I was immensely proud
and, becoming bigheaded, I
decided to write a program to
give the date of Easter Sunday
whenever the appropriate month
was requested. Many frustrating
hours later my head was back to
normal size and I sought the
help of a colleague who was also
a mathematician.

Quite a while later and after
much prodding he gave me the
formula which forms the basis of
METHOD 1.

Some 18 months later I was
chatting with an acquaintance in
my local when the subject of
computers came up and I recount-
ed the story mentioned earlier.
He then told me that he, too,
had a SPECTRUM and a program to
calculate the date of Easter
Sunday that he had copied from a
magazine and would I like to
swap programs. His program forms
the basis of METHOD 2.

Then through the letter box pops
OUTLET No. 55 containing the
letter and another formula from
John Hunter - METHOD 3.

However,when you run the program
"EASTER" [in ADDENDERS] you will
see that the three methods do
not always agree as to the
correct date of Easter Sunday.

If you go to your Local Library
and check the dates against
those given in Whittakers
Almanac, you will see that only
those dates given by Method 1
are consistently correct.

I must confess that I cannot
explain the reason for this but
I am sure that among your
readers there is someone who
can, and I am also sure that
some of them will also have some
other formula to calculate the
date of Easter.

Perhaps they could send it/them
to OUTLET for our edification.

By the way I do not seem to have
the "KWICAL" program mentioned
by John Hunter. In which issue
of OUTLET did it appear?

        Yours E.A.Hughes

P.S. Many thanks for persuading
me to treat myself to a +D for
Christmas. How did I tolerate
tape for so long?

Brian Cavers to Mr. E. A. Hughes


Many thanks. Calculating Easter
day is becoming quite a popular
interest.

The KWICAL program was in the
SAM version of OUTLET 41 only.

                          Brian.

From: Ken Stearn, FIFE

Dear Brian,

Many thanks for your reply, printed in OUTLET Issue no. 54, to my question on downloading fonts to a 24-pin printer. Unfortunately, I am still unable to get the printout I require. I used your program but just got normal printing. The fonts I have are the ones that came with OUTWRITE and I tried them as 8 and 16 bit to no avail.

I am much clearer about the whole business now but I wonder if you could explain the difference between 8 and 16-bit fonts?

I tried a Font designer in ENCELADUS Issue No. 5 and was successful in printing a downloaded font from within the program but the font was stored as a $ array. What is the difference between this and a font stored as code?

Yours sincerely,

The OUTWRITE character sets are for use on-screen in OUTWRITE itself and are nothing to do with printing. Most people have their own personal taste in text style, some like a square,blocky character, some like a thick, rounded one while others like a thin, spindly text.

The difference between the 8-bit and 16-bit characters as used in OUTWRITE are as follows...

An 8-bit set stores the design of each letter on an 8 by 8 dot matrix. For example, the letter "A" might be stored as shown at the top of the next page...

```text
........                00000000
```

.oooooo.                01111110

```text
.oo..oo.                01100110
```

.oo..oo.      or, in    01100110 .oooooo.      binary =  01111110

```text
.oo..oo.                01100110
.oo..oo.                01100110
........                00000000
```

In Mode 1, the SAM would display such a character on screen as tiny, almost invisible, dots and each dot or space would be repr- esented by one bit.

Eight bits are stored in one byte in each memory address and each byte would appear on screen as a row of eight horizontal dots (or spaces),e.g., 01100110.

In Mode 3,each dot on the screen is represented by TWO bits as it has to include colour data so TWO bytes are needed to store each horizontal slice of eight dots which make up the character design. In BASIC, the standard SAM character set is 8-bit and so the routine that PRINTs the characters on the screen has to make adjustments for each dot and this slows the routine down. In OUTWRITE,the character design is already changed into a form that can be directly used and so you will find OUTWRITE prints up a screen of text faster than SAM BASIC.The trade-off is more mem- ory is used. A 16-bit equivalent

```text
of 01100110 is 00111100 00111100
```

(if INK 3 on PAPER 0).

LPRINT AT and TAB only work in "expanded" ("text") mode - that is, after using OPEN #3;"T".They do not work after using OPEN #3; "B" which you use to send binary control codes. So, to use them with high-res graphics you need to first send the TAB using "T" then the graphics with "B",e.g.:

10 CLOSE #3 20 OPEN #3;"T" 30 LPRINT TAB 50; 40 CLOSE #3 50 OPEN #3;"B" 60 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"K";CHR$ 8; CHR$ 0; 70 FOR N=UDG"A" TO UDG"A"+7: LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N;: NEXT N

NLQ on printers relates only to the printer's own, built-in,text characters. When you send high- res graphic data you are taking over control of your printer and you, yourself need to send codes and data for higher resolution.

If you look in your printer man- ual you will see their are four different resolutions(densities) for high-res graphics: "K"(which we used in our previous example) "L", "Y" and "Z". The highest is "Z" which gives quadruple densi- ty but you must also then send each piece of UDG data FOUR TIMES after sending the "Z" code as in the example on the next page...

10 CLOSE #3: OPEN #3;"B"

20 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Z"; CHR$ 32; CHR$ 0;:REM send 32 pieces of data instead of 8

30 FOR N=UDG"A" TO UDG"A"+7

40 FOR M=1 TO 4:REM send 4 times

50 LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N;

60 NEXT M

70 NEXT N

(Anyone who didn't see last month should note that the UDG is rotated and mirrored compared to how it will show on-screen.)

If anyone wants to print eight or more UDGs together then you might not know how to calculate the two values at line 20 that state how much high-res data is about to be sent to the printer. An easy way to calculate is,eg., for 12 UDGs...

10 RANDOMIZE 32*12:REM (12 UDGS) 20 LET LO=PEEK 23670 30 LET HI=PEEK 23671

and then use...

50 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Z";CHR$ LO; CHR$ HI

For less than 8 UDGS you can use 32 times the number of UDGS for the first CHR$ and 0 for the last.

It's also worth stating here that although most printer man- uals show the value for CHR$ in brackets, e.g., CHR$ (27), both SAM and Spectrum BASIC are more advanced than many BASICs in this respect and you do not need the brackets UNLESS it is a calculated value, for example: CHR$ (X*3+2).

Наборы символов OUTWRITE предназначены для отображения на экране в самом OUTWRITE и не имеют никакого отношения к печати. У большинства людей свой личный вкус на оформление текста: кому-то нравятся квадратные, блочные символы, кому-то жирные и округлые, а третьим по душе тонкий, угловатый шрифт.

Разница между 8-битными и 16-битными символами, используемыми в OUTWRITE, заключается в следующем...

8-битный набор хранит рисунок каждой буквы в матрице 8 на 8 точек. Например, буква «A» может храниться так, как показано ниже:

```text
........                00000000
.oooooo.                01111110
.oo..oo.                01100110
.oo..oo.      или в     01100110
.oooooo.    двоичном =  01111110
.oo..oo.      виде      01100110
.oo..oo.                01100110
........                00000000
```

В Mode 1 SAM отображает такой символ на экране в виде крошечных, почти невидимых точек, и каждая точка или пробел представлена одним битом.

Восемь битов хранятся в одном байте по каждому адресу памяти, и каждый байт отображается на экране как строка из восьми горизонтальных точек (или пробелов), например, `01100110`.

В Mode 3 каждая точка на экране представлена ДВУМЯ битами, поскольку она должна содержать данные о цвете, поэтому для хранения каждого горизонтального среза из восьми точек, составляющих рисунок символа, требуется ДВА байта. В BASIC стандартный набор символов SAM является 8-битным, поэтому подпрограмма, выводящая символы по команде PRINT на экран, должна подстраивать каждую точку, что сильно ее замедляет. В OUTWRITE рисунок символа уже преобразован в форму, готовую к прямому использованию, поэтому вы заметите, что OUTWRITE выводит экран текста быстрее, чем SAM BASIC. Обратная сторона медали — расходуется больше памяти. 16-битный эквивалент строки `01100110` выглядит как `00111100 00111100` (если задан INK 3 на PAPER 0).

LPRINT AT и TAB работают только в «расширенном» («текстовом») режиме — то есть после вызова `OPEN #3;"T"`. Они не работают после `OPEN #3;"B"`, который используется для отправки бинарных управляющих кодов. Таким образом, чтобы использовать их с графикой высокого разрешения, сначала нужно отправить TAB с помощью режима «T», а затем графику с помощью «B», например:

```text
10 CLOSE #3
20 OPEN #3;"T"
30 LPRINT TAB 50;
40 CLOSE #3
50 OPEN #3;"B"
60 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"K";CHR$ 8;CHR$ 0;
70 FOR N=UDG"A" TO UDG"A"+7: LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N;: NEXT N
```

Режим NLQ на принтерах относится исключительно к собственным, встроенным текстовым символам принтера. Когда вы отправляете графические данные высокого разрешения, вы полностью берете управление принтером на себя, и вам самим нужно посылать соответствующие коды и данные для более высокого разрешения.

Если вы заглянете в руководство к своему принтеру, то увидите, что существует четыре различных разрешения (плотности) для графики высокого разрешения: «K» (которое мы использовали в предыдущем примере), «L», «Y» и «Z». Самым высоким является «Z», дающее четырехкратную плотность, но в этом случае вам также придется отправлять каждую порцию данных UDG ЧЕТЫРЕ РАЗА после посылки кода «Z», как в примере ниже:

```text
10 CLOSE #3: OPEN #3;"B"
20 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Z"; CHR$ 32; CHR$ 0;:REM отправляем 32 байта данных вместо 8
30 FOR N=UDG"A" TO UDG"A"+7
40 FOR M=1 TO 4:REM отправляем 4 раза
50 LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N;
60 NEXT M
70 NEXT N
```

(Тем, кто пропустил прошлый номер, следует помнить, что UDG для печати повернут и зеркально отражен по сравнению с тем, как он отображается на экране.)

Если кто-то захочет напечатать восемь или более UDG подряд, то может возникнуть вопрос, как рассчитать два значения в строке 20, указывающие, какой объем графических данных отправляется на принтер. Вот простой способ расчета, например, для 12 UDG:

```text
10 RANDOMIZE 32*12:REM (12 UDG)
20 LET LO=PEEK 23670
30 LET HI=PEEK 23671
```

...а затем используйте:

```text
50 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Z";CHR$ LO; CHR$ HI
```

Для менее чем 8 UDG вы можете использовать результат умножения 32 на количество UDG для первого CHR$ и 0 для последнего.

Здесь также стоит отметить, что хотя большинство инструкций к принтерам приводят значения CHR$ в скобках, например, `CHR$ (27)`, BASIC на SAM и Spectrum в этом отношении совершеннее многих других версий BASIC, и вам не нужны скобки, ЕСЛИ ТОЛЬКО это не вычисляемое выражение, к примеру: `CHR$ (X*3+2)`.

### Brian Cavers — J. Hunter

Спасибо, John. Я поместил твою «EASTER SUN» в рубрику ADD-ENDERS в этом месяце вместе с программой от E.A. Hughes под названием «EASTER», с которой ты, возможно, захочешь ее сравнить.

Используй следующий код, чтобы печатать 50 символов в строке с левым полем в 5 пробелов:

```text
10 CLOSE #3   :REM avoids errors
20 OPEN #3;"B":REM send codes
30 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"l";CHR$ 5;:
   REM left margin of 5. "l" is
   lower case L (=Left!)
50 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"Q";CHR$ 55;
   : REM right margin = 55
60 CLOSE #3:OPEN #3;"P":REM text
60 POKE SVAR 14,255: REM disable
   line length system variable
```

Этот последний POKE в данном примере не является строго обязательным, но если вы когда-нибудь попытаетесь напечатать более 80 символов в строке, например сжатым шрифтом, эта системная переменная может переопределить ваши настройки и начать новую строку после 80 символов, поэтому я обычно отключаю ее по привычке. В качестве альтернативы можно использовать саму эту системную переменную:

```text
POKE SVAR 14,50
```

...вместо установки правого поля. Это задаст фиксированную длину строки в 50 символов. Впрочем, я считаю саму системную переменную излишней помехой — это просто еще одна вещь, о которой приходится помнить, в то время как обычные коды полей принтера прекрасно работают и являются стандартными для любого компьютера.
